_meta.purpose: Berkeley-specific factual flags for Daria Wrubel, Berkeley City Council District 1, answering the East Bay for Everyone (EB4E) endorsement questionnaire. Due 2026-08-22.
_meta.scope_note: Breadth pass, one search per topic. Transit questions (service-led planning, MTC Transit Priority Policy, Connect Bay Area / AC Transit funding) deliberately excluded — covered elsewhere.
_meta.district_note: Berkeley District 1 = North/West Berkeley. Contains North Berkeley BART, the western end of Solano Ave, the San Pablo Ave and Gilman corridors, and the 8th & Harrison encampment site. Current D1 councilmember: Rashi Kesarwani. NOT the same as District 5 (Shoshana O'Keefe), which contains most of the Hopkins Street project.
_meta.confidence_key: confirmed = seen in a primary or named source; refuted = a common claim contradicted by source; unresolved = could not pin down in the time box

verification.source: Berkeley APR staff report, Table 4

verification.claim: Berkeley is far ahead on market-rate and far behind on affordable
verification.source: Arithmetic on Berkeley APR Table 4
verification.note: Above Moderate is 36.7% complete (1,344/3,664) roughly 3 years into an 8-year cycle. Very Low is 6.5% (160/2,446), Low 4.8% (67/1,408), Moderate 5.9% (83/1,416). This is the single strongest number in the file: Berkeley is on pace or better for market-rate and roughly one-fifth of pace on deed-restricted.

verification.claim: Berkeley needs roughly 1,100 units permitted per year to hit RHNA
verification.source: Berkeleyside, 'Housing production slumps in Berkeley after 2022 peak'

verification.claim: A large share of Berkeley's reported affordable RHNA progress is ADUs with ASSUMED, not actual, affordability
verification.source: Berkeley APR staff report, Table 5 and accompanying text
verification.note: HIGH VALUE. Berkeley permitted 102 ADUs in 2024 and reported them using ABAG's assumed split of 30% very low / 30% low / 30% moderate / 10% above moderate because the City does not have actual ADU affordability data. That is 31 'very low' and 31 'low' ADUs of the 78 very low and 35 low units permitted in 2024 — i.e. most of Berkeley's 2024 below-market RHNA credit is a modeling assumption, not deed-restricted units. Anyone citing Berkeley's affordable RHNA progress at face value is over-counting.

verification.claim: COMMONLY ASSERTED AND WRONG: 'Berkeley ended single-family zoning in 2021' (or 2023)
verification.source: City of Berkeley Middle Housing Zoning page; KQED; Planetizen; Berkeleyside
verification.note: HIGHEST-VALUE CORRECTION IN THIS FILE. Berkeley's February 2021 action was a RESOLUTION declaring intent to end single-family zoning (target: end of 2022). The January 2023 action was adoption of the 2023-2031 Housing Element containing the commitment. The actual binding ordinance — the Middle Housing Zoning Amendments — was not adopted until July 8, 2025 and did not take effect until November 1, 2025. Berkeley took four and a half years to convert its famous 2021 announcement into law. A candidate who repeats the 2021 framing will be corrected by an EB4E panel; a candidate who names the four-year gap demonstrates real local fluency.

verification.note: Forms allowed: duplex, triplex, fourplex, courtyard apartments and other small-scale multifamily. 35 feet is a hard cap.

verification.note: Vehicle is a 'Middle Housing zoning certificate.' This is the strongest procedural-reform fact Berkeley has, and it is exactly the kind of thing EB4E rewards. It is also a live tension for any candidate who campaigns on more neighborhood input.

verification.claim: How many units the Middle Housing ordinance has actually produced since November 1, 2025

The honest answer is 'too early, and the CY2026 APR in spring 2027 is the first real read.' Statewide experience (SB 9) is that such ordinances produce very few units; expect EB4E to probe whether the candidate knows that.

verification.claim: The 8th & Harrison encampment in West Berkeley is in District 1 and remains unresolved as of August 2026
verification.source: Berkeley Scanner, 'Why did a judge halt Harrison encampment closure?' (2026-08-06); Berkeleyside (2026-04-08)
verification.note: MOST TIME-SENSITIVE ITEM IN THIS FILE AND IT IS IN THE DISTRICT. A federal judge paused the City's latest closure plan citing three unanswered questions, days before the questionnaire deadline. The City had ordered tent residents to move by Monday, Aug 3, 2026. Verify status immediately before submitting.

verification.claim: Timeline of the Harrison litigation
verification.source: Berkeleyside and Berkeley Scanner coverage
verification.note: June 10, 2025 — federal judge (Chen) ruled the City may evict some residents but barred a full sweep, and held the City cannot take tents or vehicles used as shelter without justification and must accommodate people with disabilities under federal law. Feb 24, 2026 — City called off a planned closure. Feb 2026 — closure ordered on leptospirosis grounds. April 6-8, 2026 — judge ruled the City can clear the camp. Aug 2026 — a new closure plan halted again. Berkeley Homeless Union is the litigating party.

verification.claim: Berkeley's council loosened encampment removal rules, allowing sweeps without shelter offers
verification.source: ABC7 News; Berkeleyside, 'Berkeley considers sweeps of homeless camps without shelter offers' (2024-09-06)
verification.note: Council updated the encampment policy after the Grants Pass ruling to give staff wider authority to remove camps without making shelter offers, citing the Harrison Street encampment as a reason. This is a Berkeley council action a tenant-left-aligned candidate is likely to oppose — and it is a Berkeley-specific fact, not a general Grants Pass talking point.

verification.claim: Berkeley shelter capacity is effectively at zero
verification.source: Berkeleyside / Berkeley Scanner reporting on the Harrison closure
verification.note: Reported: six total congregate shelter beds available (four men, two women) and NO vacancies across the four motels the City acquired as non-congregate shelter. DATE OF THIS SNAPSHOT IS NOT PINNED DOWN — it is a point-in-time count, not a standing capacity figure. Verify before citing.

verification.note: CONFIRMED REFUTATION. ICC is a 501(c)(6) business league — 'Business leagues, chambers of commerce, real estate boards, etc, created for the improvement of business conditions.' Donations are NOT tax deductible. Total revenue for FY ending December 2024: $109,907,356. This matters because EB4E's Q6 framing treats model-code authorship as a private trade-association product that states are legally obliged to adopt.

verification.claim: California is required BY LAW to adopt the most recent editions of the ICC, IAPMO and NFPA model codes each triennial cycle
verification.source: California Building Standards Commission, CALCode Quarterly
verification.note: THE CORE POINT OF EB4E'S Q6. The state has no discretion to skip a cycle; it adopts the 2024 ICC editions and the 2023 NEC as the base, then amends. So a private 501(c)(6) trade association effectively writes California's baseline building code, and cost-increasing model-code changes flow through automatically unless the state or a local jurisdiction affirmatively amends them out.

verification.result: confirmed (as a flag; the underlying facts are verified above)
verification.source: Berkeleyside 2026-05; Darrell Owens substack
verification.note: The Planning Commission SCALED BACK the corridors upzone after neighborhood backlash. Solano Avenue's 617-unit capacity is the D1 piece. EB4E will almost certainly ask whether the candidate supports the fuller version, and whether she would vote against her own district's homeowners. Hedging here is the most likely single point of failure. Related: Council must adopt by roughly December 2026 or risk Housing Element non-compliance and Builder's Remedy exposure — Owens frames it exactly that way.

verification.claim: FLAG 2 — Berkeley's Middle Housing ordinance is ministerial and NON-APPEALABLE to ZAB or Council
verification.source: City of Berkeley Middle Housing Zoning page
verification.note: A candidate who campaigns on 'preserving Berkeley's unique character' and community input will be asked whether she would keep ministerial approval and the appeal ban. Her own site's framing ('preserving Berkeley's unique character') sits awkwardly next to it. This is the sharpest process question available.

verification.claim: FLAG 3 — TOPA is a real YIMBY/tenant-left fault line in Berkeley and Council already rejected it
verification.result: confirmed (on the Berkeley history); unresolved (on EB4E's own position)
verification.source: Daily Cal; KQED; EBHO
verification.note: Berkeley Council FAILED TO ADOPT TOPA at a special meeting in October 2024, with a majority citing the City's financial and administrative capacity — NOT ideology. That is the important nuance: the stated Berkeley objection was 'we cannot administer or fund this,' which is a fiscal argument, not an anti-tenant one, and it is still available as a challenge. Opposition was led by Berkeley Property Owners Association (Krista Gulbransen). EBHO supports TOPA. NO EB4E POSITION ON TOPA FOUND — do not assume they oppose it. Nationally, YIMBY-tenant friction on TOPA is about transaction delay, not principle.

verification.claim: FLAG 4 — Sanctioned encampments have a documented Berkeley funding hole
verification.source: Berkeley 2025-05-20 Item 29; Berkeley Scanner
verification.note: The existing Berkeley sanctioned-camp proposal has no funding mechanism and the City faces a deficit in a key homeless-services source. A pro-sanctioned-encampment answer needs a Berkeley-specific funding answer or it reads as unserious. Note also that the sanctioned-camp proposal came from O'Keefe — who is the leading council opponent of the Hopkins bike lanes — so the coalition alignments here do not map neatly onto YIMBY/NIMBY.

verification.claim: FLAG 5 — Hopkins is a loyalty test in and adjacent to District 1, just resolved
verification.source: Berkeley Scanner; Berkeleyside; Owens
verification.note: Walk Bike Berkeley and the Sierra Club are the aligned orgs; the D1 incumbent Kesarwani was the lead sponsor. Any D1 candidate who is soft on Hopkins, or who leads with the 145 parking spaces, will be read as Save Hopkins-adjacent. Conversely, the project is not built until 2027-28 repaving, so 'would you defend it if it is reopened' is a fair and likely question.

verification.claim: FLAG 6 — the affordable-vs-market-rate framing trap
verification.source: Berkeley APR Table 4
verification.note: Berkeley's shortfall is overwhelmingly in the deed-restricted tiers (5-7% of allocation) while market-rate is at 37%. A tenant-left-aligned candidate's natural instinct is to say 'we need affordable, not luxury.' EB4E's counter is that market-rate is the only category actually being produced and that constraining it does not produce affordable units. Both facts are true. The data supports either frame, which is why the candidate needs to hold both.

verification.claim: FLAG 7 — fees and the stalled pipeline
verification.source: Berkeley Inclusionary staff report; Berkeleyside stall coverage
verification.note: Berkeley has collected $51M+ in mitigation fees since 2016 and inclusionary yields 15% of units built, while zero housing projects are under construction downtown. The obvious YIMBY question is whether she would reduce or defer fees/inclusionary to unstick projects. That directly conflicts with EBHO and the tenant-left. NOTE: the sources found attribute the stall to interest rates, construction costs, labor and lending — NOT to fees. That is a defensible factual position and it is city-and-press-sourced.

verification.claim: FLAG 8 — labor standards as a cost driver
verification.source: General YIMBY/building-trades tension; no Berkeley-specific instance found
verification.note: INFERRED ONLY. YIMBY groups frequently oppose prevailing-wage and skilled-and-trained-workforce mandates as cost drivers; a former AFT organizer may be pressed on this. But AFT is a teachers' union, not the building trades, so the link is weak and NO Berkeley-specific fight was found. Do not treat this as a documented flag.

verification.note: EB4E is a housing/transit organization. Nothing found suggesting they take positions on ALPR/surveillance. Low risk; likely simply out of scope for the questionnaire.
